IENT is a B2B procurement platform that brings together apps for processes such as Purchase Requisitions, Invoices, Contracts, and other procurement workflows.

It helps companies manage how they source, purchase, and pay for the materials and services needed to run their business.

Business requirement

Bring RFQ and Auction into the Existing platform

To expand the platform's sourcing capabilities, we were introducing two new apps: RFQ and Auction.

The requirement was to build both apps within the existing ecosystem, leveraging its established patterns, functionalities, and workflows rather than creating standalone experiences.

RFQ
Auction
A little about RFQ and Auction

Two ways to run a sourcing Event

RFQ

Request for Quotation

Buyers invite vendors to quote against a requirement, then weigh each quotation on price, terms and delivery.

1234

Auction

Vendors bid against each other within a set window, seeing their rank and the lead bid as the Event runs.

While the two apps differ in how vendors compete, both follow a common sourcing process: defining a requirement, inviting vendors, collecting responses, evaluating them, and reaching an outcome.

The Gap

What the existing app structure could not carry

Most of the functionality these apps needed already fit within the platform’s existing app structure. What was missing was a place for the core sourcing activity itself.

The missing Event layer

01

We found that this interaction aligned with the established concept of a sourcing Event, where:

  • Buyers publish sourcing requirements
  • Suppliers respond or bid
  • The buyer evaluates responses before making an award

02Vendor responses, bidding, response comparison, and awarding were not simply additional features. Together, they formed a distinct interaction with its own lifecycle, participants, rules, and outcome.

This became the missing Event layer within our existing app structure.

Research

Understanding the Event

Synthesized from SAP Ariba, Coupa, CIPS, and Gartner to establish a common definition for the project.

What is an Event?

A structured sourcing activity where buyers engage vendors to collect, compare, and evaluate responses for a purchasing requirement.

Across the different sourcing formats, the Event consistently consists of a few fundamental elements:

01
Requirement
What the buyer needs sourced: specs, terms, and line items.
02
Participants
The vendors invited to take part in the Event.
03
Response
The quotes or bids vendors submit against the requirement.
04
Evaluation
The buyer comparing responses across the field.
05
Outcome
The award that closes the Event and names the winner.
The two roles
Buyer

Sourcing Specialist

Role
Runs sourcing events on behalf of the organization.
Needs to
Define requirements, invite vendors, collect responses, compare submissions, and award business.
Goals
  1. Get competitive vendor responses
  2. Make a defensible sourcing decision
  3. Complete the Event efficiently
  4. Maintain control over rules and timelines
Vendor

Sales / Bid Representative

Role
Responds to buyer sourcing events on behalf of their company.
Needs to
Understand requirements, submit a compliant quotation or bid, and monitor the Event.
Goals
  1. Clearly understand what the buyer needs
  2. Submit an accurate response
  3. Stay competitive
  4. Avoid missing deadlines or requirements
The established lifecycle

Studying how mature tools such as SAP Ariba run a sourcing event, I folded its lifecycle states into one Event with three stages, sitting between creation and completion.

Mapping the Event

Three stages, from actions to requirements

I broke the Event into three stages. In each, I mapped what the buyer and the vendor do, then turned those actions into what the product has to provide.

Intent

Give the vendor a clear view of the requirement before participating.

02Running

Buyer

  • Tracks who leads and by how much
Experience

A live view of the competition: who leads, how bids move, and the gap between them.

Vendor

Buyer

Direction

One place for the Event layer

With the requirements clear, the next question was where the Event layer should live.

Scattering it across existing functionalities would break one continuous sourcing interaction into disconnected parts. It needed a single, dedicated home.

We introduced a new Response Tab within both Auction and RFQ, alongside the existing tabs. This extended the existing structure rather than replacing it, giving the Event a single place to live and bringing the entire sourcing interaction together for both buyers and vendors.

Approach

What the design had to hold

01A structured way to compare responses

Buyers judge many responses, not one. A list and detail layout lets them move across vendors while the selected response stays in view.

02Event context, always in sight

Every action depends on where the Event stands. A quick summary keeps the key information on screen for each role, so no one leaves the tab to check.

03A live view that stays current

Bids change throughout the Event. Both roles see the latest state as it happens, without interrupting their work, which keeps bidding competitive.

04Tools to work the responses, not just read them

An Event gathers a large volume of sourcing information across vendors. Event and response tools let buyers synthesise, compare and act on it.

The flow

Laid end to end, the actions mapped across the three stages form one flow through the Event. The buyer opens it and branches to edit details, review and award, or download. The vendor opens it to submit or revise.

Solution

From research to shipped design

The research gave direction. What follows is how that direction became a working design: the journeys that scoped the tab's job, the lifecycle that shaped its behaviour, the four decisions that set its structure, and the shipped result.

The layout

Two panels, one for each side

1234567
The Base Design

What these decisions produced

The Base Design

What these decisions produced

Scheduled01 / 08
01 · Scheduled

Before the Event opens

The buyer’s view of an Event before it goes live. The tab provides key information to both buyers and vendors, allowing vendors to review the Event and prepare their responses in advance.

02 · Scheduled

Where the Event is in its life

The stage and time remaining until the Event opens are displayed alongside the title, giving every user an immediate understanding of the Event’s current status and what to expect next.

03 · Scheduled

The Event in one strip

The summary bar holds the figures that define the Event: lead bid, starting value, increment, responses received and closing date. Before the Event opens it reserves their place. Once it goes live, it updates as bids arrive, so the buyer reads the progress of the whole Event without opening a single response.

04 · Scheduled

Actions on the whole Event

Download all Responses and the comparative statement report sit outside the response panel. They act on every vendor at once, and their position says so.

05 · Scheduled

The whole field at a glance

Every vendor at summary level: name, bid and rank. The buyer scans the field and picks one without losing sight of the rest. Vendors who have not responded sit one click away, at the foot of the list.

06 · Running

Once the Event goes live

The same tab, now live. The status turns to Live and counts down to close; the layout holds, and what changes is what the buyer reads and does.

07 · Running

Depth on the selected response

This is the vendor’s complete response, shown exactly as submitted for the buyer to review. The response panel adapts to whatever the Event requires, allowing different response forms to use the same layout.

08 · Closed

Once the Event closes

The last stage. Bidding has stopped, every response is final, and the buyer moves from watching the field to deciding it. Award Vendor now appears beside View all Past Response Versions, inside the panel, so the decision is made on the response it affects.

Validation

Then Konica came

The design was built to adapt, but adaptability only proves itself in real‑world use.

Konica, one of the first enterprise customers to adopt the Response Tab, put that flexibility to the test.

Their procurement process went beyond simply selecting a winner, exposing new requirements that expanded what the tab needed to support.

What the requirement changed

Before Konica, a closed Event went straight to the award. Konica placed an evaluation stage and a voting stage between them, each owned by a different role.

Konica based screens
More than awarding
The decision was no longer a single award. Department leads rated each response against weighted criteria, a steering committee voted on those scores, and the managing director gave final approval before the award.
An AI summary for every response
With more reviewers reading the same responses, each needed the substance fast. Every response now carries an AI summary, opened from inside the response panel, so a reviewer can grasp it before reading it in full.

This is where the early decisions paid off.

Because the action slot and information panels were already role‑aware and permission‑driven, Konica's actions slotted into the existing structure.

The slot already shipped with Award as its default; selecting a preferred vendor, voting, and approving simply joined it.

No structural redesign. Their process became a configuration, not a custom build.

How the decisions held

Each decision, tested by a real requirement

DecisionWhat Konica testedHow it held
01Two-column layout
What Konica tested

More roles now reviewed the same responses.

How it held

The compare-left, detail-right frame carried all of them. No new layout needed for the extra reviewers.

Held
02The action slot
What Konica tested

Award was joined by Vote and Select Preferred Vendor.

How it held

These button actions dropped into the existing slot. Placement still signalled scope, no exceptions added.

Held
03Structure to scale
What Konica tested

The requirement brought more fields, and an entire scoring section, into the response.

How it held

The grouped, sectioned structure absorbed them, including the rating grid as a new section, without the layout breaking.

Held

One requirement proved the principle twice.

Konica's department leads needed to rate each vendor against weighted criteria, but a rating means nothing without seeing the weight behind each criterion. The weightage itself was set elsewhere in the product, not in the tab.

So the Response Tab pulled that weightage in and displayed it as read-only context (visible only to the department lead, only at the scoring stage) alongside the inputs to rate each vendor.

It was the same principle behind the shared key-info panel, proven a second time: one surface, showing different information to different roles based on permission and stage. Two independent instances of the same idea, which is what made it a principle, not a one-off.
